lines.text: ==== documents/meridian-negotiation-guidelines.docx ====

012: (b) All material amendments to existing GMRAs and MRAs, including amendments that modify haircut levels, margin provisions, events of default, cross-default thresholds, substitution rights, repricing triggers, governing law, or dispute resolution mechanisms;

018: •  Meridian acts as Seller in substantially all repo transactions contemplated by these guidelines. The positions and ranges set forth herein are calibrated to Meridian's role as Seller. In the rare circumstance that Meridian acts as Buyer, the desk must consult with the General Counsel before applying these guidelines, as certain provisions (including haircut targets and substitution rights) may require adjustment.

022: •  These guidelines are informed by Meridian's audited net capital of $412,000,000 as of 31 December 2024, as determined in accordance with SEC Rule 15c3-1 (the "Net Capital Rule") under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended. All thresholds expressed as percentages of net capital are calculated on that basis and must be re-evaluated upon each quarterly net capital recertification. The Office of the CFO circulates quarterly net capital certifications to the desk, the General Counsel, and Risk Management within five business days following the end of each fiscal quarter. If a quarterly recertification reveals a change in net capital that would alter the dollar amounts implied by percentage thresholds set forth herein (e.g., the cross-default walk-away analysis in Section 7.1), the desk must coordinate with the General Counsel to determine whether an interim revision of these guidelines is warranted.

026: 2.1 — Overriding Objective. Meridian's overriding objective in repo documentation negotiations is to maintain operational flexibility in collateral management while preserving robust netting and close-out protections. Operational flexibility — particularly the ability to substitute collateral without undue delay or counterparty consent, to manage margin calls within reasonable timeframes, and to avoid unnecessary repricing events during the life of a transaction — is essential to the efficient functioning of Meridian's secured funding business. At the same time, the integrity of netting and close-out provisions is critical to Meridian's regulatory capital treatment and insolvency protections. Negotiators must balance these two objectives and should not sacrifice one in pursuit of the other.

030: •  Walk-away positions represent hard limits. Acceptance of terms beyond walk-away thresholds is prohibited without Managing Director and General Counsel joint approval, which will be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only after a written assessment of the commercial rationale and risk impact has been prepared and presented to both approvers. Walk-away overrides are expected to be rare; if the desk finds itself seeking walk-away overrides on a recurring basis with a particular counterparty or class of counterparties, the guidelines themselves may need to be revised, and the desk should raise this with the General Counsel.

034: 2.6 — Regulatory Awareness. All negotiation positions and settlement outcomes must be consistent with Meridian's obligations under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Certain terms — particularly haircut levels, cross-default thresholds, and margin provisions — have a direct impact on Meridian's regulatory net capital computation. Negotiators are not expected to perform net capital calculations themselves but must be aware of the interaction between documentation terms and net capital requirements and must escalate any term that could have a material capital impact to the Office of the CFO through the procedures set forth in Section 9.
035: Section 3 — Haircuts (Pricing Rate / Purchase Price Discount)

036: Haircut levels — referred to in certain GMRA contexts as the "Pricing Rate" or "Purchase Price Discount" and in certain MRA contexts as the "Margin Percentage" — are among the most commercially significant terms in a repo agreement. The haircut determines the relationship between the Market Value of collateral delivered by the Seller and the Purchase Price received by the Seller. A higher haircut means the Seller receives less cash for a given amount of collateral, effectively increasing the Seller's cost of funding and reducing the efficiency of its collateral deployment.

037: For purposes of these guidelines, "haircut" refers to the percentage by which the Purchase Price is discounted relative to the Market Value of the Purchased Securities. All illustrative calculations in this Section assume a simple one-minus-haircut formulation — i.e., Purchase Price = Market Value × (1 − Haircut) — unless otherwise indicated.

039: Sovereign collateral is Meridian's primary collateral class for repo transactions and receives the most favorable haircut treatment from bank counterparties due to its high credit quality and deep secondary market liquidity.

040: Target: Haircut of 1.5% or lower. At this level, $100,000,000 in sovereign collateral at Market Value produces a Purchase Price of approximately $98,522,167.49 (reflecting minor rounding adjustments for accrued interest and settlement date conventions that may apply in practice). The 1.5% target is consistent with haircut levels observed in bilateral repo transactions between U.S. broker-dealers and well-capitalized bank counterparties during the period from January 2024 through September 2024.

041: Acceptable: Haircut up to 2.0%. The desk may agree to any figure at or below 2.0% without escalation. A midpoint settlement of 1.75% is a reasonable compromise and should be offered as a counter when the counterparty opens at 2.0% or above. At 1.75%, illustrative sovereign collateral with a Market Value of $100,000,000 yields a Purchase Price of approximately $98,280,098.28 (subject to the same rounding and convention adjustments noted above). The difference between the target of 1.5% and the acceptable ceiling of 2.0% represents a range of approximately $500,000 in funding efficiency per $100,000,000 of collateral deployed — a meaningful but manageable cost within the desk's trading parameters.

042: Walk-away: Haircuts above 2.0% for sovereign collateral are not acceptable. Any counterparty insistence on a sovereign haircut above 2.0% must be escalated per Section 9. In practice, a sovereign haircut above 2.0% from a well-capitalized bank counterparty is unusual and may indicate that the counterparty's credit or risk function has classified Meridian at an elevated risk tier, which should prompt a broader relationship discussion rather than a narrow documentation negotiation.
043: Eligible Sovereign Issuers: The following sovereign issuers are eligible for the haircut levels specified above:

051: All eligible sovereign issuers must be rated A– (Standard & Poor's) / A3 (Moody's Investors Service) or above by at least one of the two foregoing rating agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction. If the sovereign credit rating of any G7 issuer falls below the minimum threshold during the life of a Transaction, the impact on existing positions must be assessed by Risk Management in consultation with the desk. The inclusion or exclusion of specific sovereign issuers in Annex I is a material negotiation point and should be confirmed with the desk before finalizing any agreement.

053: Corporate collateral is Meridian's secondary collateral class for repo transactions. Due to the higher credit risk and lower secondary market liquidity of corporate debt securities relative to sovereign collateral, bank counterparties apply larger haircuts to corporate collateral.

054: Target: Haircut of 3.5% or lower. At this level, $50,000,000 in corporate collateral at Market Value produces a Purchase Price of approximately $48,309,178.74. The 3.5% target is achievable with well-capitalized bank counterparties where the corporate collateral pool consists predominantly of investment-grade issues with short-to-medium residual maturities.

055: Acceptable: Haircut up to 4.5%. The desk may agree to any figure at or below 4.5% without escalation. A midpoint settlement of 4.25% is a reasonable compromise and should be offered when the counterparty opens at 5.0% or above. At 4.25%, illustrative corporate collateral with a Market Value of $50,000,000 yields a Purchase Price of approximately $47,961,630.70. The desk should note that the spread between the target (3.5%) and the acceptable ceiling (4.5%) is wider for corporate collateral than for sovereign collateral, reflecting the greater variability in market practice for corporate haircuts and the desk's need for additional negotiation room.

056: Walk-away: Haircuts above 4.5% for corporate collateral are not acceptable without escalation. Escalation must follow the procedures set forth in Section 9. Haircuts above 4.5% for investment-grade corporate collateral are indicative of an aggressive counterparty risk posture that warrants further review.
063: 3.3 — Haircut Negotiation Notes

066: (b) Certain counterparties may propose tiered haircut schedules that assign different haircut levels to different sovereign issuers (e.g., a lower haircut for U.S. Treasuries and a higher haircut for Italian government bonds). The desk may agree to reasonable tiered schedules provided that (i) all individual haircut levels fall within the ranges specified in Section 3.1 and (ii) the weighted average haircut across the projected collateral pool does not exceed the acceptable ceiling of 2.0%.

067: (c) Haircut levels directly affect Meridian's net capital charges under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Haircuts materially above the acceptable range increase the capital charge on repo positions because the excess haircut represents a deduction from net capital. Any haircut level that would result in incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital charges in excess of $5,000,000 in aggregate across the projected transaction portfolio with the relevant counterparty must be flagged to the Office of the CFO before the desk or outside counsel conveys agreement to the counterparty. This escalation requirement applies regardless of whether the haircut level is within the acceptable range specified in this Section 3.

068: (d) The desk should avoid agreeing to haircut "reopener" or "reset" provisions that allow the counterparty to unilaterally increase haircuts during the life of a Transaction upon the occurrence of specified triggers (e.g., a rating downgrade of the Eligible Collateral issuer or a market volatility event). Such provisions transfer pricing risk to Meridian mid-transaction and are operationally disruptive. If a counterparty insists on a haircut reset mechanism, the desk should propose instead that any increased haircut apply only to new Transactions entered into after the trigger event, not to existing Transactions.

070: Margin provisions govern the mechanics of collateral adjustments during the life of a Transaction and are central to both parties' credit protection. The key margin provisions addressed in this Section are the Margin Threshold (the de minimis amount below which margin calls need not be made), margin call timing and settlement, and the Net Exposure Cap.
071: 4.1 — Margin Thresholds (Delivery Amounts)

072: The Margin Threshold (sometimes referred to as the "Minimum Transfer Amount" or "Delivery Amount Threshold") is the minimum Net Exposure that must exist before either party is obligated to deliver margin. Thresholds that are too low generate a high volume of small margin calls that impose disproportionate operational costs; thresholds that are too high leave excessive uncollateralized exposure.

073: Target: $500,000 symmetric — that is, a Margin Threshold of $500,000 applies equally to both Seller's and Buyer's obligation to deliver margin. The symmetric formulation is commercially balanced and straightforward to administer. At a $500,000 threshold and an assumed average transaction size of $250,000,000 to $500,000,000, margin calls will be triggered only when Net Exposure exceeds a de minimis level, reducing operational friction without creating material credit exposure.

074: Acceptable: Asymmetric thresholds, provided the Seller (Meridian) Margin Threshold is no lower than $500,000. In practice, certain bank counterparties — particularly those with large settlement operations and automated margin call systems — seek lower thresholds to minimize their uncollateralized exposure to non-bank counterparties. The desk may agree to a Buyer Margin Threshold as low as $250,000 where the counterparty insists on asymmetry — that is, a $500,000 threshold for Seller (Meridian) deliveries and a $250,000 threshold for Buyer (counterparty) deliveries. This asymmetric formulation benefits the counterparty by requiring Meridian to deliver margin at a lower threshold when the counterparty is owed margin, while preserving Meridian's $500,000 threshold when Meridian is owed margin. The desk should agree to this formulation only if the counterparty provides a reasonable commercial justification and should note in the negotiation record that the asymmetry was conceded.

075: Walk-away: Any Seller Margin Threshold below $500,000 is not acceptable without escalation. A Seller Margin Threshold of less than $500,000 — and in particular, thresholds of $250,000 or less for Seller deliveries — would subject Meridian to frequent small-value margin calls that impose disproportionate operational burden on Meridian's New York–based operations and settlement teams. The operational cost of processing and settling margin calls at low thresholds (including settlement instruction preparation, DTC or Clearstream delivery execution, and internal booking and reconciliation) can be significant in aggregate, particularly across a large portfolio of outstanding Transactions with a single counterparty. If a counterparty insists on a Seller Margin Threshold below $500,000, the desk must escalate per Section 9.
087: Section 5 — Substitution of Collateral

088: Substitution rights are among the most important provisions in a GMRA or MRA from Meridian's perspective as Seller. The ability to substitute collateral — that is, to deliver replacement Purchased Securities and receive back the original Purchased Securities during the life of a Transaction — is essential to Meridian's collateral management and portfolio optimization functions. Without adequate substitution rights, collateral pledged under a repo is effectively trapped for the duration of the Transaction, limiting Meridian's ability to respond to changing market conditions, client demand, or internal portfolio rebalancing needs.
089: 5.1 — Substitution Rights

090: Target: Unilateral right of substitution by Seller on 1 business day's prior notice to Buyer, without requirement for Buyer consent. Under this formulation, Meridian may deliver substitute collateral of equivalent or greater Market Value and receive back the original Purchased Securities, subject only to the condition that Meridian provide at least one full business day's advance written notice of the substitution. No conditions beyond the notice requirement would apply — Meridian would have full discretion to determine the composition of substitute collateral, subject only to the requirement that the substitute collateral constitute Eligible Collateral under the terms of Annex I. This target position maximizes Meridian's operational flexibility and is commercially appropriate in transactions where the Buyer's economic interest is in the repo rate rather than in the specific identity of the collateral.
091: Acceptable: Seller's right of substitution on 1 business day's notice, subject to the following conditions:

092: (a) Substitute collateral must fall within the same or a better Eligible Collateral category as the original Purchased Securities. For purposes of this condition, sovereign collateral is a "better" category than corporate collateral. Accordingly, substitution of sovereign collateral for corporate collateral is permitted (a substitution "up"), but substitution of corporate collateral for sovereign collateral is not permitted (a substitution "down"). This condition protects the Buyer against collateral quality deterioration during the life of the Transaction while preserving Meridian's ability to manage its collateral inventory within a given quality tier.

093: (b) No Margin Deficit exists at the time of the proposed substitution. This condition ensures that Meridian is not using the substitution mechanism to avoid or defer a margin call. If a Margin Deficit exists, Meridian must first satisfy the margin call and then, once the Margin Deficit has been eliminated, may exercise its substitution right. This is a reasonable condition that aligns the incentives of both parties.

094: (c) No prior consent of Buyer is required. This is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. The distinction between a substitution right that is subject to conditions (acceptable) and a substitution right that requires Buyer consent (not acceptable) is fundamental. A conditional substitution right preserves Meridian's control over the timing and execution of the substitution; a consent-based substitution right transfers that control to the Buyer and introduces the risk of delay or refusal, which is operationally unacceptable.

095: Walk-away: Any requirement for Buyer's prior written consent to substitution is unacceptable. Such a provision effectively converts the repo into a pledge structure from an operational perspective, even if the legal characterization as a sale and repurchase is preserved. If the Buyer must consent before Meridian can substitute collateral, Meridian's collateral management team cannot reliably plan or execute portfolio rebalancing, and the practical utility of the substitution right is severely impaired. The desk must not agree to a consent requirement under any circumstances without escalation to the Managing Director and the General Counsel under the walk-away override procedures described in Section 9.3.

096: If a counterparty insists on consent rights, the desk should explain that the "same-or-better" collateral quality condition and the "no Margin Deficit" condition described above adequately protect the Buyer's interests. The Buyer's credit exposure is unaffected by a substitution that delivers collateral of equivalent or better quality and value, and the Buyer's protection against undercollateralization is preserved by the no-Margin-Deficit condition. Consent mechanisms introduce unacceptable operational delay — particularly in cross-border transactions where the Buyer's credit and operations teams may be in different time zones from Meridian's operations desk — and serve no legitimate protective function that is not already addressed by the two conditions described above.

099: (a) European bank counterparties commonly open by requiring Buyer's prior written consent to any substitution. This is a standard opening position in European bank playbooks and should not be treated as a walk-away trigger for the negotiation as a whole. Instead, the desk should counter with the acceptable formulation described in Section 5.1 (conditional substitution without consent) and explain the commercial rationale. In the experience of the desk, most European bank counterparties will ultimately accept the conditional formulation after one or two rounds of negotiation.

100: (b) Some counterparties may propose a middle ground in which consent is required only for substitutions that involve a change in collateral category (e.g., from sovereign to corporate) but not for substitutions within the same category. This middle ground may appear reasonable but is unnecessary if the "same-or-better" condition is in place, as that condition already prohibits downward substitutions. The desk should point this out and insist on the clean conditional formulation without any consent overlay.

102: (d) The desk should ensure that the substitution mechanics in Annex I are drafted to provide for "simultaneous exchange" — that is, the delivery of substitute collateral and the return of original collateral should occur on the same settlement date and, where possible, through delivery-versus-delivery (DVP) or free-of-payment (FOP) mechanisms that minimize settlement risk for both parties. The desk should not agree to formulations that require Meridian to deliver substitute collateral one or more settlement cycles before receiving back the original collateral, as this would create a "gap" period during which Meridian has outstanding deliveries on both sides of the substitution.
103: Section 6 — Repricing

104: Repricing provisions allow one or both parties to adjust the Purchase Price of an outstanding Transaction to reflect changes in the Market Value of the Purchased Securities or changes in prevailing market repo rates during the Transaction's term. From Meridian's perspective as Seller, in-term repricing introduces operational complexity and potential P&L volatility, particularly where repricing triggers a cash payment obligation (either a payment by Meridian to the counterparty if the Market Value of the collateral has declined, or a return of cash by the counterparty to Meridian if the Market Value has increased). The desk's objective is to minimize repricing frequency while acknowledging that bank counterparties with term repo exposures have a legitimate interest in periodic repricing to manage their balance-sheet exposure.
105: 6.1 — Repricing Rights

106: Target: Repricing available only at maturity roll — that is, no in-term repricing right for either party during the life of an individual Transaction. Under this formulation, the Purchase Price set at the inception of a Transaction would remain fixed throughout the Transaction's term, and any adjustment to pricing would occur only when the Transaction matures and is rolled into a new Transaction (if applicable). This target position eliminates the operational burden of in-term repricing and provides Meridian with pricing certainty for the duration of each Transaction.

107: Acceptable: Quarterly repricing or repricing on the 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date, whichever occurs later, with no less than 2 business days' prior written notice by the requesting party. The desk may agree to either a quarterly cycle (i.e., repricing on the 91st, 182nd, and 273rd calendar day from the Purchase Date, or the next business day if such date falls on a non-business day) or a 90-day cycle (i.e., repricing on each 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date). Where the counterparty proposes both triggers — for example, repricing on each calendar quarter-end and on each 90th calendar day — the "whichever is later" formulation ensures that Meridian is not subject to repricing more frequently than quarterly. The desk should insist on this qualifier in all cases where both triggers are proposed.

108: The 2 business day notice period is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. It provides Meridian's operations team with adequate time to source replacement collateral, adjust positions, prepare cash for any repricing payment, and coordinate with settlement systems. The 2 business day period also allows for at least one full business day of internal processing after receipt of the repricing notice, accounting for the possibility that the notice is received near end-of-day.

109: Walk-away: Any repricing frequency more often than quarterly — including but not limited to monthly repricing, bi-weekly repricing, weekly repricing, or on-demand repricing at the counterparty's sole discretion — is not acceptable. In-term repricing at sub-quarterly frequency imposes significant operational and P&L volatility on the desk and is disproportionate to the counterparty's legitimate risk management needs. Sub-quarterly repricing must be escalated under the walk-away procedures described in Section 9, and approval is expected to be granted only in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., a transaction with an unusually long tenor and unusual collateral characteristics that justify more frequent adjustments).

112: (a) Bank counterparties conducting term trades in excess of 60 calendar days will uniformly resist Meridian's target of repricing only at maturity roll. The desk should expect to concede this point early in the negotiation and move promptly to the acceptable position. Protracted insistence on the "repricing at maturity only" target in the face of clear counterparty resistance is unlikely to be productive and may consume negotiation capital that is better deployed on other issues.

113: (b) The critical protection for Meridian in the acceptable position is the 2 business day notice period. This notice period provides adequate time for the desk to source replacement collateral, calculate and prepare any cash payment, and execute settlement instructions. Do not agree to notice periods shorter than 2 business days under any circumstances. A 1 business day notice period — or, worse, a "same-day" notice period — would compress Meridian's operational response time below acceptable levels, particularly for repricing events that involve EUR-denominated collateral settling through Clearstream.

114: (c) Where the counterparty's opening position is a 90th calendar day repricing option (as is common under European bank playbooks, particularly for Swiss and German bank counterparties), a reasonable compromise is to accept the 90th day trigger but add the quarterly alternative, with the "whichever is later" qualifier, to smooth timing and ensure that repricing does not occur more frequently than once per quarter. This compromise gives the counterparty its preferred 90-day trigger while protecting Meridian against the possibility that the 90-day cycle and the quarterly cycle could produce overlapping repricing events in quick succession.

115: (d) The desk should be aware that some counterparties may propose repricing triggers that are linked to external events rather than fixed time periods — for example, repricing upon a credit downgrade of the Eligible Collateral issuer, a specified decline in the Market Value of the collateral, or a significant move in benchmark repo rates. Such event-driven repricing triggers are generally unacceptable because they introduce uncertainty about the timing and frequency of repricing and can result in multiple repricing events in a short period during market stress. The desk should resist event-driven triggers and should propose that the counterparty's concerns be addressed through the margin provisions (which already provide for collateral adjustment in response to market value changes) rather than through the repricing mechanism.

117: Events of Default provisions define the circumstances under which a party's obligations under the GMRA or MRA may be accelerated and the close-out netting mechanism invoked. Properly calibrated Events of Default are essential both to protect Meridian against a counterparty's creditworthiness deterioration and to prevent Meridian from being subject to premature or unjustified close-out by the counterparty. The two Events of Default that are most frequently the subject of negotiation are the Cross-Default provision and the Act of Insolvency grace period.
118: 7.1 — Cross-Default

119: The Cross-Default provision in a GMRA or MRA provides that a default by a party under any other agreement (typically, a default in payment of indebtedness above a specified threshold) constitutes an Event of Default under the GMRA or MRA, even if no default has occurred under the GMRA or MRA itself. Cross-Default provisions are a standard feature of GMRA and MRA documentation and serve as an early-warning mechanism — they permit the non-defaulting party to close out and exercise its netting rights before the defaulting party's financial condition deteriorates further. However, the Cross-Default threshold must be set at a level that captures only material defaults; a threshold that is too low can trigger cascading defaults across Meridian's entire agreement portfolio in response to minor or technical payment failures.

120: Target: Cross-Default threshold of $50,000,000 for both parties. At Meridian's audited net capital of $412,000,000 (31 December 2024), $50,000,000 represents approximately 12.14% of net capital — a level that captures only material payment failures and is well above the range of routine mark-to-market fluctuations, operational payment delays, and minor settlement failures that can occur in the ordinary course of Meridian's business. The $50,000,000 target is Meridian's preferred opening position and should be included in all first drafts.

121: Floor (Acceptable): $25,000,000. This represents approximately 6.07% of Meridian's net capital. The desk may agree to any cross-default threshold at or above $25,000,000 without CFO sign-off. A $25,000,000 threshold is a reasonable compromise that still provides a meaningful buffer against cascading defaults triggered by non-material events. The desk should offer $25,000,000 as a midpoint counter-offer early in the negotiation when the counterparty opens below the target, with the goal of closing on this figure and avoiding a protracted back-and-forth on the cross-default issue.

122: CFO Sign-off Required: Any cross-default threshold below $25,000,000 but at or above $15,000,000 requires the prior written approval of Meridian's Chief Financial Officer. Requests for CFO approval must be submitted in writing (email to the CFO with copies to the Managing Director and the General Counsel) and must include a memorandum setting out:
123: (a) The counterparty's rationale for seeking a threshold below $25,000,000 — including any regulatory, risk management, or credit policy considerations cited by the counterparty;

124: (b) The number and aggregate notional of existing agreements in Meridian's documentation portfolio with cross-default thresholds below $25,000,000, together with a list of the relevant counterparties and the applicable threshold for each agreement. This information is necessary to assess the aggregate cascading-default risk across Meridian's portfolio — if a material number of existing agreements already have low cross-default thresholds, the incremental risk of adding another such agreement is magnified;

125: (c) The incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital impact, if any, of a lower cross-default threshold. While the cross-default threshold itself does not directly generate a net capital charge, a lower threshold increases the probability of an Event of Default being triggered, which could in turn require Meridian to take reserves or charges against its net capital computation in connection with close-out or unwind scenarios; and

126: (d) The desk's recommendation, including any proposed conditions or mitigants (e.g., a higher threshold that applies only to Meridian's obligations, or a cure period that applies before the Cross-Default is triggered).

127: Walk-away: Any cross-default threshold below $15,000,000 is not acceptable under any circumstances. At $15,000,000, the threshold would represent less than 3.64% of Meridian's audited net capital — a level at which routine mark-to-market losses, minor operational payment failures, or ordinary-course settlement disputes could trigger cascading defaults across Meridian's agreement portfolio. The systemic risk to Meridian of a low cross-default threshold is disproportionate to the incremental credit protection it provides to the counterparty, particularly given that the counterparty's primary protection in a repo transaction is the collateral itself, supplemented by margin provisions. Negotiators must not agree to a cross-default threshold below $15,000,000 even with escalation; this is a hard walk-away, and no override is available. If a counterparty refuses to accept a threshold at or above $15,000,000, the desk should inform the General Counsel and the Managing Director, and the negotiation should be paused pending a senior-level commercial discussion about whether the counterparty relationship can proceed on other terms.
128: 7.2 — Cross-Default Negotiation Notes

130: (a) European bank counterparties with large CET1 capital bases — for example, Voss Bank AG, which reported CET1 of CHF 8,300,000,000 as of 31 December 2024 — routinely propose low cross-default thresholds, often in the range of $10,000,000 to $15,000,000. The rationale cited by such counterparties is that these amounts are immaterial relative to their own balance sheets and that their standard credit playbooks require low thresholds for non-bank counterparties. The desk should explain to such counterparties that the cross-default threshold must be calibrated to Meridian's capital base, not the counterparty's. A $10,000,000 threshold that is immaterial to a bank with CHF 8,300,000,000 in CET1 capital is manifestly not immaterial to a broker-dealer with $412,000,000 in net capital, and the cascading-default risk of a $10,000,000 threshold is borne entirely by Meridian. This is a straightforward and well-understood argument, and most European bank counterparties will accept it when presented clearly and early in the negotiation.

131: (b) Offer the $25,000,000 midpoint as a compromise early in the negotiation to avoid protracted discussion on this issue. Cross-default threshold negotiations can consume disproportionate time and attention relative to their commercial significance, and the desk is better served by closing on this point quickly at $25,000,000 and reserving its negotiation capital for issues such as substitution rights and repricing.

132: (c) The desk should be alert to counterparty proposals that define "indebtedness" broadly for purposes of the Cross-Default provision — for example, proposals that include trade payables, margin obligations under other agreements, or contingent liabilities (such as guarantees) within the definition of "indebtedness." The desk should resist such expansive definitions and should insist that "indebtedness" for Cross-Default purposes be limited to borrowed money and debt securities, which is the standard GMRA formulation. An expansive definition of "indebtedness" effectively lowers the functional cross-default threshold by increasing the universe of obligations that can trigger the provision.

133: (d) Where the counterparty proposes a "cross-acceleration" provision rather than a true "cross-default" provision, the desk may consider this as a more favorable alternative, as cross-acceleration requires not merely a default under the other agreement but an actual acceleration of the obligations under that agreement. Cross-acceleration provides the counterparty with less aggressive protection than cross-default (because a default may exist for some time before acceleration occurs), but it is commercially reasonable and reduces the risk of cascading defaults triggered by technical or curable defaults. The desk may offer cross-acceleration as a compromise if the counterparty resists the $25,000,000 cross-default threshold.
134: 7.3 — Act of Insolvency Grace Period

135: The Act of Insolvency provision in a GMRA or MRA provides that the occurrence of certain insolvency-related events — including the filing of a bankruptcy petition (whether voluntary or involuntary), the appointment of a receiver or liquidator, the making of an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or the admission in writing of an inability to pay debts as they come due — constitutes an Event of Default. The key negotiation issue is whether the Act of Insolvency Event of Default is triggered immediately upon the occurrence of the insolvency event or whether the affected party is entitled to a grace period to cure the event before it ripens into an Event of Default.

136: Target: 30 calendar days' grace period for curing an Act of Insolvency. Under this formulation, the occurrence of an insolvency-related event does not constitute an immediate Event of Default if the event is cured, dismissed, or vacated within 30 calendar days. A 30-calendar-day grace period provides Meridian with substantial time to respond to an involuntary bankruptcy petition (which may be frivolous or unfounded), to correct an administrative error in a regulatory filing, or to take other appropriate action to resolve the insolvency event. This target is aggressive and is unlikely to be accepted by most bank counterparties without significant concession, but it establishes a strong opening position.

137: Acceptable: 10 to 15 business days. The desk may agree to any grace period within this range without escalation. A 15 business day period is the preferred position within the acceptable range and should be the desk's counter-offer when the counterparty opens at zero days (immediate Event of Default) or at a grace period shorter than 10 business days. A 10 business day period is the floor of the acceptable range and should be agreed to only after the counterparty has demonstrated clear resistance to 15 business days. At 10 business days, Meridian would have approximately two calendar weeks (accounting for weekends and assuming no intervening holidays) to respond to an insolvency event, which is the minimum period that the General Counsel considers adequate for a meaningful response — including engagement of bankruptcy counsel, preparation and filing of a motion to dismiss an involuntary petition, and coordination with regulatory authorities.

138: Walk-away: Any grace period shorter than 5 business days is not acceptable. A zero-day grace period — that is, an immediate Event of Default upon the occurrence of an Act of Insolvency with no opportunity to cure — is a hard walk-away. Such provisions expose Meridian to the risk that an administrative error in an insolvency-related filing, a frivolous or vexatious involuntary bankruptcy petition filed by a disgruntled creditor, or a technical event that satisfies the definition of "Act of Insolvency" without reflecting genuine financial distress triggers an immediate close-out before Meridian has any opportunity to respond, seek dismissal of the petition, correct the error, or otherwise address the situation. An immediate close-out triggered by a technical insolvency event could result in significant losses to Meridian (due to the forced liquidation of collateral at unfavorable prices), reputational damage, and potential regulatory consequences. The 5 business day absolute floor provides the minimum window necessary for Meridian to assess the situation and initiate a response.
139: 7.4 — Act of Insolvency Grace Period Negotiation Notes

143: (c) Some counterparties may propose a differentiated grace period that provides a longer cure period for involuntary insolvency events (e.g., involuntary bankruptcy petitions filed by third parties) and a shorter cure period — or no cure period — for voluntary insolvency events (e.g., voluntary bankruptcy filings or admissions of inability to pay debts). This differentiated approach has commercial logic: the counterparty's concern about immediate termination is greatest for involuntary events, where the affected party may be an innocent victim of a frivolous filing. The desk may consider a differentiated grace period as a creative compromise, provided that (i) the grace period for involuntary events is at least 15 business days and (ii) the grace period for voluntary events is at least 5 business days. Such a differentiated formulation should be offered only if the counterparty has firmly resisted a uniform grace period within the acceptable range.

144: (d) The desk should ensure that the grace period language is drafted to apply to the "occurrence" of the Act of Insolvency rather than to the "knowledge" of the Act of Insolvency. A knowledge-based trigger creates ambiguity about when the grace period begins to run and can lead to disputes about when a party became aware (or should have become aware) of the insolvency event. An occurrence-based trigger is cleaner and more certain.
145: Section 8 — Governing Law, Jurisdiction, and Dispute Resolution
151: 8.2 — Jurisdiction and Dispute Resolution

152: Preferred: Non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales for GMRAs, or the courts of the State of New York and the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York for MRAs. Non-exclusive jurisdiction preserves each party's right to bring proceedings in any court of competent jurisdiction while establishing a primary forum for the resolution of disputes. Exclusive jurisdiction clauses are disfavored because they limit Meridian's flexibility to pursue claims or enforcement actions in the forum most convenient or effective under the circumstances (e.g., the jurisdiction in which the counterparty's assets are located). However, if a counterparty insists on exclusive jurisdiction, the desk may agree to exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales (for GMRAs) or the courts of the State of New York and the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York (for MRAs) without escalation.

153: Acceptable — if arbitration is required: LCIA arbitration with London as the seat. Some bank counterparties — particularly European bank counterparties headquartered in civil law jurisdictions — strongly prefer arbitration over court litigation for the resolution of disputes under financial documentation. Where a counterparty insists on an arbitration clause, the desk may agree to LCIA (London Court of International Arbitration) arbitration, provided that the following conditions are met:

155: (b) The LCIA Rules' expedited procedure must apply to all claims with an amount in dispute of $5,000,000 or less. This cap ensures that low-value disputes — including margin call disputes, minor calculation disagreements, interest computation disputes, and similar operational-level controversies that may arise in the ordinary course of a repo relationship — are resolved efficiently and cost-effectively through an expedited single-arbitrator proceeding rather than through full three-arbitrator proceedings with extended briefing schedules, discovery, and oral hearings. The LCIA's expedited formation rules (Article 9A of the LCIA Rules) provide for the appointment of a sole arbitrator, abbreviated procedural timetables, and a decision within a compressed timeframe, all of which are well-suited to the resolution of small-value disputes.

156: (c) The arbitration clause must expressly preserve each party's right to seek interim or provisional relief from a court of competent jurisdiction, including injunctive relief and attachment of assets, pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal. This carve-out is standard in LCIA arbitration clauses and should not be controversial, but the desk should confirm that it is included in the final text.
157: Walk-away: The following dispute resolution mechanisms are not acceptable:

158: •  ICC arbitration (International Chamber of Commerce arbitration) is not acceptable. ICC arbitration proceedings are significantly more expensive than LCIA proceedings, involve more complex administrative requirements (including advance payment of the full estimated costs of the arbitration), and historically take longer to reach a final award. The General Counsel has determined that the ICC's cost structure and procedural complexity are not appropriate for disputes arising under Meridian's repo documentation.

159: •  Ad hoc arbitration (i.e., arbitration not administered by any recognized institution) is not acceptable. Ad hoc arbitration lacks the procedural safeguards, administrative support, and established rules that are provided by institutional arbitration, and it creates a heightened risk of procedural disputes, delays in the appointment of arbitrators, and challenges to the enforceability of awards.

160: •  Any arbitration clause that does not include an expedited procedure for small claims is disfavored and should be resisted. If a counterparty proposes LCIA arbitration without the expedited procedure carve-out, the desk should insist on including the carve-out as a condition of agreeing to arbitration. If the counterparty refuses the expedited procedure carve-out, the desk should escalate to the General Counsel before agreeing to a "full" LCIA arbitration clause without any small-claims mechanism.

163: (a) European bank counterparties, particularly those headquartered in Switzerland (including Voss Bank AG and similarly situated institutions), strongly prefer LCIA arbitration over court litigation. This preference is driven by a combination of factors, including the confidentiality of arbitration proceedings (which is important to Swiss banks subject to bank secrecy obligations), the neutrality of London as a seat, and the enforceability of LCIA awards under the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. The desk should expect to encounter this preference in a significant majority of European bank GMRA negotiations and should be prepared to concede court jurisdiction in favor of LCIA arbitration, provided that the expedited procedure carve-out for claims of $5,000,000 or less is obtained.

164: (b) The $5,000,000 expedited procedure cap is a firm position. It has been calibrated by the General Counsel to align with LCIA's own expedited formation rules and reflects the General Counsel's assessment of the dispute-value threshold below which full three-arbitrator proceedings are disproportionately costly and time-consuming. The desk should not agree to a lower cap (which would subject more disputes to the expedited procedure, potentially to the detriment of Meridian's interests in disputes that require full proceedings) or a higher cap (which would subject fewer disputes to the expedited procedure and reduce the efficiency benefits of the carve-out) without General Counsel approval.

165: (c) If a counterparty proposes LCIA arbitration with a seat other than London — for example, Zurich, Geneva, or Paris — the desk should resist and insist on London. The London seat is essential for the reasons described in Section 8.2(a) above. If the counterparty insists on a continental European seat, the desk must escalate to the General Counsel.

166: (d) The desk should be aware that certain counterparties may propose multi-tier dispute resolution mechanisms that require the parties to engage in negotiation or mediation before commencing arbitration. Such mechanisms can introduce delay and additional cost and are generally disfavored. However, a short mandatory negotiation period (e.g., 30 calendar days from the date of a dispute notice) before commencement of arbitration is acceptable and may be offered as a concession if it helps secure the counterparty's agreement to the LCIA expedited procedure carve-out.
171: •  Sovereign haircuts at or below 2.0% (Section 3.1);
172: •  Corporate haircuts at or below 4.5% (Section 3.2);
173: •  Symmetric or asymmetric margin thresholds with a Seller Margin Threshold at or above $500,000 (Section 4.1);
175: •  Conditional substitution without Buyer consent (Section 5.1);
176: •  Quarterly or 90-day repricing with a "whichever is later" qualifier and at least 2 business days' notice (Section 6.1);
177: •  Cross-default thresholds at or above $25,000,000 (Section 7.1);
178: •  Act of Insolvency grace periods of 10 to 15 business days (Section 7.3);
180: •  Non-exclusive court jurisdiction or LCIA arbitration with the expedited procedure carve-out for claims of $5,000,000 or less (Section 8.2); and

185: (a) Cross-default threshold below $25,000,000 but at or above $15,000,000 (Section 7.1). The request must be accompanied by the memorandum described in Section 7.1, addressing the counterparty's rationale, the existing portfolio of low-threshold agreements, and the incremental net capital impact.

186: (b) Any haircut level that would result in incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital charges in excess of $5,000,000 in aggregate across the projected transaction portfolio with the relevant counterparty. The desk should coordinate with the Office of the CFO to model the net capital impact of proposed haircut levels before conveying agreement. If the desk is uncertain whether a proposed haircut level crosses the $5,000,000 threshold, it should request a preliminary estimate from the Office of the CFO before responding to the counterparty.

192: (b) Any dispute resolution mechanism other than non-exclusive court jurisdiction (as described in Section 8.2) or LCIA arbitration with the expedited procedure carve-out for claims of $5,000,000 or less (as described in Section 8.2). This includes, without limitation, ICC arbitration, ad hoc arbitration, expert determination, mediation as a sole remedy, or any other non-standard dispute resolution mechanism.

194: (d) Walk-away overrides — that is, any proposal to agree to a term that falls below a "Walk-away" threshold identified in these guidelines — require the joint approval of the Managing Director (Dana R. Castellano) and the General Counsel. Walk-away overrides will be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only after a written assessment of the commercial rationale, risk impact, and regulatory implications has been prepared and presented to both approvers. The desk should not seek walk-away overrides as a routine matter; the walk-away thresholds are set at levels that reflect the General Counsel's and Risk Management's considered judgment, and routine overrides would undermine the integrity of these guidelines.

197: •  Cross-default threshold below $15,000,000 (less than 3.64% of Meridian's net capital as of 31 December 2024). As discussed in Section 7.1, a cross-default threshold at this level creates unacceptable systemic risk of cascading defaults across Meridian's agreement portfolio. No override is available.

198: •  Act of Insolvency grace period below 5 business days. As discussed in Section 7.3, a grace period below 5 business days — and in particular, a zero-day grace period — does not provide Meridian with minimally adequate time to assess and respond to an insolvency event. No override is available.

234: •  EUR-denominated Eligible Collateral: Clearstream Banking S.A. ("Clearstream"). All deliveries and receipts of EUR-denominated Purchased Securities and substitute collateral should be effected through Clearstream. Meridian maintains a Clearstream account for this purpose. Clearstream settlement operates on a Central European Time cycle, and negotiators should be mindful of the time-zone differential when agreeing to margin call cut-off times and substitution notice periods.

{"command":"python - <<'PY'
from zipfile import ZipFile, ZIP_DEFLATED
from lxml import etree
from copy import deepcopy
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime

base=Path('documents/turn-2-redline-meridian.docx')
out=Path('output/turn-3-redline-gmra.docx')
out.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
W='http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main'
R='http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships'
CT='http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/content-types'
NS={'w':W,'r':R}

def q(n): return f'{{{W}}}{n}'
def rtag(n): return f'{{{R}}}{n}'

def ttext(el, deleted=False):
    return ''.join(el.xpath('.//w:delText/text()' if deleted else './/w:t/text()', namespaces=NS))

def visible_text(p):
    # after accepting revisions, all visible text is in w:t; exclude field/instruction complications
    return ''.join(p.xpath('.//w:t/text()', namespaces=NS))

def clone_rpr(p):
    r=p.find(q('r'))
    if r is not None:
        rp=r.find(q('rPr'))
        if rp is not None: return deepcopy(rp)
    rp=etree.Element(q('rPr'))
    fonts=etree.SubElement(rp,q('rFonts')); fonts.set(q('ascii'),'Times New Roman'); fonts.set(q('hAnsi'),'Times New Roman')
    sz=etree.SubElement(rp,q('sz')); sz.set(q('val'),'22')
    szc=etree.SubElement(rp,q('szCs')); szc.set(q('val'),'22')
    return rp

def make_run(text, p, deleted=False, bold=False):
    r=etree.Element(q('r'))
    rp=clone_rpr(p)
    if bold and rp.find(q('b')) is None: etree.SubElement(rp,q('b'))
    r.append(rp)
    tx=etree.SubElement(r,q('delText') if deleted else q('t'))
    if text.startswith(' ') or text.endswith(' ') or '  ' in text: tx.set('{http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}space','preserve')
    tx.text=text
    return r

def clear_content(p):
    for child in list(p):
        if child.tag != q('pPr'):
            p.remove(child)

def add_plain(p,text,bold=False):
    p.append(make_run(text,p,bold=bold))

def add_container(p, kind, text):
    el=etree.Element(q(kind))
    el.set(q('id'), str(add_container.next_id)); add_container.next_id += 1
    el.set(q('author'),'Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP')
    el.set(q('date'),'2025-04-17T17:00:00Z')
    el.append(make_run(text,p,deleted=(kind=='del')))
    p.append(el)
    return el
add_container.next_id=1000

def replace_clean(p,text):
    clear_content(p); add_plain(p,text)

def replace_tracked(p,new,comment_id=None):
    old=visible_text(p)
    clear_content(p)
    if old:
        add_container(p,'del',old)
    if comment_id is not None:
        start=etree.Element(q('commentRangeStart')); start.set(q('id'),str(comment_id)); p.append(start)
    add_container(p,'ins',new)
    if comment_id is not None:
        end=etree.Element(q('commentRangeEnd')); end.set(q('id'),str(comment_id)); p.append(end)
        rr=etree.Element(q('r')); rr.append(etree.Element(q('commentReference'))); rr[0].set(q('id'),str(comment_id)); p.append(rr)

def replace_tracked_old_new(p,old,new,comment_id=None):
    clear_content(p)
    if old:
        add_container(p,'del',old)
    if comment_id is not None:
        start=etree.Element(q('commentRangeStart')); start.set(q('id'),str(comment_id)); p.append(start)
    if new:
        add_container(p,'ins',new)
    if comment_id is not None:
        end=etree.Element(q('commentRangeEnd')); end.set(q('id'),str(comment_id)); p.append(end)
        rr=etree.Element(q('r')); rr.append(etree.Element(q('commentReference'))); rr[0].set(q('id'),str(comment_id)); p.append(rr)

with ZipFile(base,'r') as zin:
    files={name:zin.read(name) for name in zin.namelist()}
root=etree.fromstring(files['word/document.xml'])
# Accept all Turn 2 revisions first: this makes agreed Turn 2 drafting and the three resolved issues clean.
for d in list(root.xpath('//w:del',namespaces=NS)):
    par=d.getparent()
    if par is not None: par.remove(d)
for ins in list(root.xpath('//w:ins',namespaces=NS)):
    par=ins.getparent()
    if par is None: continue
    idx=par.index(ins)
    for child in list(ins):
        par.insert(idx,child); idx+=1
    par.remove(ins)
ps=root.xpath('//w:body/w:p',namespaces=NS)

replace_clean(ps[11],'Turn 3 redline prepared by Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP on behalf of Seller against the Turn 2 redline dated 28 March 2025.')
replace_clean(ps[12],'Mark-up by Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP, 570 Lexington Avenue, 30th Floor, New York, NY 10281, USA, on behalf of Seller.')
replace_clean(ps[13],'Turn 3 treatment: Issues 1–3 resolved in clean text; Issues 4–7 advanced in tracked changes; 7 agreed drafting marks accepted clean; 9 pending drafting marks retained in tracked changes and flagged for Calder Stone / Voss Bank attention.')

replace_clean(ps[232],'Haircut Percentage: 1.75% (the "Sovereign Haircut").')
replace_clean(ps[233],'Application: The Purchase Price for a Transaction in which the Purchased Securities are Eligible Sovereign Securities shall be determined by dividing the Market Value of such Purchased Securities (as of the relevant Purchase Date or, in the case of Additional Purchased Securities, as of the date of transfer) by 1.0175.')
replace_clean(ps[234],'Illustrative example: If the Market Value of Eligible Sovereign Securities is $100,000,000, the Purchase Price shall be $100,000,000 ÷ 1.0175 = $98,280,098.28.')
replace_clean(ps[236],'Haircut Percentage: 4.25% (the "Corporate Haircut").')
replace_clean(ps[237],'Application: The Purchase Price for a Transaction in which the Purchased Securities are Eligible Corporate Securities shall be determined by dividing the Market Value of such Purchased Securities (as of the relevant Purchase Date or, in the case of Additional Purchased Securities, as of the date of transfer) by 1.0425.')
replace_clean(ps[238],'Illustrative example: If the Market Value of Eligible Corporate Securities is $50,000,000, the Purchase Price shall be $50,000,000 ÷ 1.0425 = $47,961,630.70.')

replace_clean(ps[61],'4.4 Upon the existence of a Margin Deficit, Buyer may by notice to Seller (a "Margin Call") require Seller to transfer to Buyer Additional Purchased Securities or Cash Margin (or any combination thereof) in an amount sufficient to eliminate such Margin Deficit (the aggregate amount so required, the "Delivery Amount"). replace_clean(ps[62],'4.5 Upon the existence of a Margin Excess, Seller may by notice to Buyer (also a "Margin Call") require Buyer to transfer to Seller Equivalent Securities or Cash Margin (or any combination thereof) sufficient to eliminate such Margin Excess (the aggregate amount so required, the "Return Amount"). # Resolved Issue 3 — clean conditional, no-consent substitution mechanics.
replace_clean(ps[98],'8.1 Subject to the provisions of Annex II, Section 9, Seller may from time to time during the term of any Transaction effect a substitution of Alternative Securities for all or any part of the Purchased Securities in that Transaction.')
replace_clean(ps[99],'8.2 Any notice of substitution shall be made by Seller to Buyer in writing (including by electronic mail) and shall specify the Purchased Securities to be replaced, the proposed Alternative Securities (including ISIN, nominal amount, issuer, coupon, maturity, and credit rating), and the proposed date on which the substitution is to take effect.')
replace_clean(ps[101],"8.3 Seller shall give Buyer not less than one (1) Business Day's prior notice of any proposed substitution. No consent of Buyer shall be required.")
replace_clean(ps[102],"8.4 The substitution shall be effected on the Business Day specified in Seller's notice by the simultaneous transfer of the Alternative Securities by Seller to Buyer (or to Buyer's account at the relevant settlement system) and the transfer of the relevant Purchased Securities by Buyer to Seller (or to Seller's account at the relevant settlement system), in each case in accordance with the provisions of Paragraph 6.")
replace_clean(ps[103],'8.5 Alternative Securities must qualify as Eligible Collateral, must be of the same or better Eligible Collateral category as the Purchased Securities being replaced, and must satisfy all of the eligibility criteria set out in Annex II, Section 3. replace_clean(ps[261],'(a) Seller may, from time to time during the term of any Transaction, effect a substitution of Alternative Securities for all or any part of the Purchased Securities in that Transaction.
